units: a damp place high up gathers several natural settings within a small stretch
a plant carpet soaked with water rims the pool
organisms clinging to stone withstand the lack of water
hollow stems serve as shelter for young insects
the water looks clear but carries plant debris
small almost see-through animals move in short bursts
seeds buried in the bottom wait for a favorable spell
each level depends on the others and losing one makes the whole poorer
text: A mountain bog crowds several very different settings into one small patch of ground. Right at the water's edge lies a carpet of moss, soaked through and spongy, which gives way under a boot and closes over again at once. Above it the bare rock wears a coat of gray lichen, rough under the thumb, able to ride out one drought after another. In between stand tall grasses whose hollow stems shelter tiny larvae. The water counts as a setting of its own. It looks clear on top, yet stir it and a cloud of shredded plant matter comes up. See-through insects dart through it in short jerky bursts, almost impossible to spot. Deeper down, under the silt, seeds lie asleep and wait for a kinder season to sprout. Every layer leans on the others, and take one out and the whole place grows poorer.

units: artificial lighting was aimed first at the safety of public ways
it then spread to buildings and parking areas
commercial signs shine at night over empty walkways
only the strongest bodies in the sky stay visible
an orange glow hides the depth of the sky
birds on migration circle lit-up buildings
insects active after sundown die near the lamps
some communities have already switched the lighting off in the middle of the night without complaint
text: Let us be honest about it: we lost the sky without ever noticing. Street lighting came first, for safety, and that much holds up. Then it spread to building fronts, parking lots, storefronts and crossings, and everyone found that normal. Shop signs took to burning all night over sidewalks with nobody on them. What is left overhead? A scatter of the brightest bodies in the sky, and behind them an orange wash where the depth used to be. Migrating birds steer by starlight, so they circle lit towers instead. Night-flying insects wear themselves out against the lamps and die at the foot of the posts. We could switch off after midnight and nothing would fall apart. Whole communities have tried it, and not one voice was raised against it. It would be a pity to wait until the dark is a memory before missing it.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman leading the team explores a network of galleries not yet mapped
a fall into a crack during her childhood set off her calling
she discovered then a chamber crossed by falling water
her parents worked a dry sloping plot
she understood that the water missing at the surface was moving lower down
she trained in a field devoted to the study of water
her measurements show the deep reserves refilling faster than expected
the neighboring communities changed their water intakes after these results
text: The researcher who runs the team spends her weeks under rock, in a maze of galleries no survey had ever put on paper. Her calling began with a fall. As a child she slipped into a narrow crack in the family pasture and landed in front of a chamber where water came down in a sheet. Her parents worked a dry slope, so she grasped early that whatever went missing at the surface was moving along just beneath it. She went off to study water itself, then came back to measure what she had glimpsed. Her readings showed the deep reserves refilling far faster than anyone had assumed, and the settlements nearby rewrote their intake plans because of it. The map she keeps updating now serves as an argument for farmers and officials alike, and her quiet manner no longer keeps people from listening.

units: the exhibition deals with the deep sea
the first room shows animals kept in a liquid
this display conveys neither the pressure nor the darkness of the depths
the end of the route makes up for that flaw
a dark passage forces the visitor to move forward blind
projected images show jelly-like animals overhead
a trembling of the floor goes with that scene
the writer regrets that this choice was not applied from the start
text: You come out of this deep-sea show feeling you have brushed against something vast and been poorly served. The weakness hits you in the opening room. Case after case lines up pale specimens set in alcohol, with nothing to suggest the pressure or the darkness they came from. Under a hard lamp, a glowing fish is nothing more than one more jar. The closing stretch of the route makes up for the blunder. Here the designers dug out a dark corridor where you feel your way forward while projections send drifting jellyfish high across the ceiling. The floor trembles faintly underfoot. At last you get the effect they were after, a crushing body of water with rare creatures adrift in it. Had that choice been made at the door, the whole thing would have won over even the most distracted visitor.

units: the sender reports on two methods for tracking freshwater animals
the first method uses catching devices sunk in the water
the second consists in laying boards on the ground
the underside of the boards holds the moisture
the sunken devices take more grown individuals
they call for regular visits and sometimes injure the animals' limbs
the boards give fewer catches but steadier records
a grainy material spread under the boards favors the young ones
the sender suggests splitting the two methods over two separate sectors
text: Dear colleague, I owe you an account of the two protocols we settled on for tracking the pond amphibians. The first relies on smooth-walled traps sunk in the water. The second uses boards laid flat on the ground, whose rough underside keeps a film of moisture. Traps take more adults, but somebody has to walk the line every other evening, and the animals often come out with damaged legs. Boards go down once and draw only whatever is looking for cover, so the yield drops while the data comes out cleaner. One more thing is worth passing on. The grainy layer we spread under the boards seems to suit the young ones and to bother the grown ones. If you agree, let us keep the boards on the upper sector and the traps on the lower one, then set the catches side by side once the season closes.

units: a handful of forest soil shelters a great many living things
the combined work of those beings produces fertility
threads coming from fungi extend the reach of the roots
these threads take in water and dissolved minerals
they receive in exchange sugary compounds made by the foliage
the tearing of that network lets the rain carry off the surface layer
bringing a damaged soil back takes tens of years
the measures named include covering with plant waste and cutting down machine traffic
dark springy crumbs show that the soil is recovering
text: What lives in a handful of forest soil? Fungal threads, bacteria, mites and worms by the thousand, and it is their combined work that builds the fertility of the place. What do those threads do? They stretch the reach of tree roots, draw in water and dissolved salts, then trade them for the sugars the leaves have made. What happens when that web tears? The ground loses its grip, rain carries off the top layer, and whatever grows back comes up thin. Can a damaged plot be brought back? Yes, provided you are willing to accept a scale of several decades. Cover the surface with plant waste, keep the heavy machines off it, bring in deep-rooted plants that open channels again. What tells you the effort has worked? Dark springy crumbs that come apart between the fingers without crumbling into dust.

units: the forest keeper advises coming before the female returns
the group sets out in the dark without a light
the assistant notices that the nest hole sits higher than the year before
the keeper climbs with a ladder
he draws out of the hole a young bird covered in soft feathers
the bird cannot stand up yet
three other chicks fill the hollow
the visitors measure the feathers and look at the shade of the beak
the female comes back to the nest shortly after the group leaves
text: The forest keeper had warned us the day before: “Come before the mother takes up her rounds again,” so we set out ahead of dawn with no lamp, finding the path by the sound of our own steps on it. At the foot of the beech his assistant whispered that the hole opened higher up than the year before. The keeper hauled the ladder into place, climbed it, slid a hand inside and drew out a chick still in soft down, not yet able to hold itself up on its feet. “Three more behind it,” he said, and settled the bird back at the bottom of the nest. We took the length of the feathers and the shade of the beak, and moved nothing else. On the way down he boiled his trade down to watching, counting and going away again. The mother was back soon after we left, as though nothing had happened.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: quarry workers found remains of shellfish in a stone lying high up
these shapes were put down at first to a whim of the rock
cutters observed that the remains stacked up in a steady order
that stacking recalled the floor of calm water
the same order showed up in different valleys
the explanation by chance became hard to believe
observers put forward that the stone had taken shape under water
this idea assumed a lifting of the ground
the idea was accepted because its forecasts held up in the field
text: Picture the quarry workers who split a slab far above the sea and found shells running right through the stone. For generations the marks were put down to a whim of the rock, which people said could mimic living things. Then some of the more curious cutters noticed that the shells sat in layers, in a steady order, much the way they settle on the floor of a quiet bay. Since the same order turned up in one valley after another, chance grew hard to believe in. A few observers came out with an unwelcome account. The rock had taken shape under water, and the ground had risen afterwards. The idea took decades to get through, because it meant admitting that the land itself moves. It won in the end because its forecasts held: where it promised sea layers, sea layers were found.

units: a watercourse boxed in between straight walls sheds its water too fast
the water reaches the lower ground all at once during heavy rain
the low parts of the built-up areas are flooded
the bed dries out with the first spell of strong heat
the straight line had been dug to win farming ground
that line did away with the bends that slowed the water and let it soak in
putting things right means handing back to the watercourse part of the room it once had
the work includes tearing out the built banks and planting trees again
the overflows turn less violent and a flow stays on through the dry spell
text: A river running straight between two concrete walls sheds its water faster than it should. Hydrologists say the same thing after every flood. The flow reaches the lower ground all at once, swamps the low-lying blocks, then drains away, and the bed dries out with the first heat wave. That straight cut was dug to win farming ground, and it did away with the bends where the water used to slow down and soak in. The fix now being tried is to hand the river back part of the room it once had. Crews break up the built banks, reopen old side channels, and plant trees whose roots hold the edges together. The water winds again, spreads across meadows made to flood, and works its way down to the water table. Floods lose their punch, and a thread of water stays in the bed through the dry months.

units: the walkers climb a steep face and come down by the other
the face they climb is dry and rocky
only short grasses grow in the cracks of the rock
the walkers' water supplies empty fast during the climb
the change of face happens within a few steps at the top
the other face is covered with thick growth
very cold water runs from the wall
a group of farm animals rests in the shade on that side
the narrator concludes that a height is made of faces exposed in different ways
text: We had decided to climb the steep face and come down by the other, with no notion of how far the two faces would contradict each other. The way up was dry and stony, all hot slabs and tufts of short grass wedged into the cracks, with the rasp of insects for company. Nothing up there held water, and our bottles emptied while we watched. The switch took about three steps. Past the ridge the slope opened out thick and green, carpeted with ferns, the air smelling of wet moss. Threads of water seeped from the wall, cold enough to numb a hand. We came upon a herd grazing in the shade while behind us the other pitch went on baking. One mountain, cut by a single crest, kept two climates and two sets of tenants. Since that walk I no longer look at high ground as a single solid mass.
